column11: a real count of real US patients, and it is a FLOOR not an estimate. Burton BK, Ficicioglu C, Pedro H, Eisengart JB, Botha J, Pathak R, Robinson I, Wright E, Muenzer J, Mol Genet Metab 2026;149(3):110281 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2026.110281, PMID 42868950), the Hunter Outcome Survey: 'The US cohort comprised 326 patients with MPS II (median ages at symptom onset and at diagnosis of 1.5 year and 3.0 years, respectively).' The other available US count is 207 MPS II patients in the National MPS Society registry over 1995 to 2015 (Puckett Y, Mallorga-Hernandez A, Montano AM, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2021;16(1):241, doi 10.1186/s13023-021-01880-8, PMID 34051828, PMC8164808), whose authors state 'National MPS Society data may not include all MPS patients within the US as patients are not required to be a member of the society'
column12: BOTH AVAILABLE COUNTS ARE VOLUNTARY-REGISTRY ENROLMENTS, so both are floors on the living US population, and the larger is carried. THE WIDELY QUOTED '629 US MPS II PATIENTS' IS NOT USED AND SHOULD NOT BE: it originates in a paywalled tertiary clinical overview as an editorial back-calculation from an incidence range multiplied by a life-expectancy assumption, with no primary study behind it. The Puckett paper's own prevalence rate of 0.70 per 1,000,000 is circular - it is just its 207 cases divided by its average US population - so it adds no independent information

column11: the US federal evidence review for newborn screening, which states both the rate and the newborn denominator. Ream MA, Lam WKK, Grosse SD et al., 'Evidence and recommendation for mucopolysaccharidosis type II newborn screening in the United States', Genet Med 2023;25(2):100330 (doi 10.1016/j.gim.2022.10.012, free full text at stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/124428/cdc_124428_DS1.pdf): 'based on the case detection rate through usual clinical care of 0.67 per 100,000 live births, only 24 cases of MPS II of any phenotype (range: 5-78) would be identified' on 3.6 million US newborns
column12: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS THE ONE NOT USED. The same review models universal newborn screening at 1.6 per 100,000 births: 'there would be 480 positive screens (range: 346-523), 59 cases of MPS II of any severity identified (range: 44-61) ... 322 false positives (range: 131-352)'. The US is therefore under-ascertaining MPS II by roughly 60% under usual care. 24 is the detected inflow, which is the right number for a commercial pool today; 59 is what the inflow becomes if MPS II is added to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel, and that would be a step change in this asset's addressable population. Note also that MPS II is X-linked and essentially male-only: the 0.67 per 100,000 is per ALL live births, and the per-male-birth figure is 1.3 per 100,000 (Wraith JE et al., Eur J Pediatr 2008;167(3):267-277, PMC2234442), which is the same thing expressed on half the denominator. Do not multiply them together

column11: the neuronopathic share, which is the population RGX-121 is built for: NCT07236606's primary outcome is 'Efficacy of RGX-121 on Neurodevelopmental Function (as measured by the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, 3rd Edition)' (the book's trials table, asset 3052), a CNS endpoint. Ream MA et al., Genet Med 2023;25(2):100330, the US federal evidence review cited above: 'Approximately 60% of people with MPS II have the severe or neuronopathic form of the disease.' 326 x 0.6 = 196 US patients, and 24 x 0.6 = about 14 neuronopathic births a year detected under usual care
column12: three other free sources bracket it. Wraith 2008 (PMC2234442): 'Two-thirds of patients present with CNS involvement, representing the more severe end of the disease phenotype.' A US retrospective chart review of 140 patients (J Health Econ Outcomes Res 2022, doi 10.36469/jheor.2022.33801, PMID 35620452, PMC9098230): 'Overall, 87 patients (62.1%) had a record of cognitive impairment documented in their charts.' The Hunter Outcome Survey US cohort itself is the low end: 'Data on cognitive status after 5 years of age were available for 166 patients, of whom 73 (44.0%) had cognitive impairment' - lower partly because it measures documented impairment in survivors with data past age 5, which censors the most severely affected. 60% is the US federal review's own figure and is taken; 44% is the downside case

column12: A BORROWED RATE, AND THE TWO DISEASES DIFFER IN WAYS THAT CUT BOTH WAYS. Higher here: MPS II's existing therapy, idursulfase enzyme replacement, does not cross the blood-brain barrier and so does nothing for the neuronopathic disease this layer counts, where Elevidys competes against an entrenched steroid standard and two other gene therapies. Lower here: the eligible pool is about 196 patients against Duchenne's 3,982, so a single centre's referral pattern moves the rate by percentage points, and the pool is geographically scattered across a disease most paediatric neurologists see once in a career. THE ENROLMENT IS A WARNING: NCT07236606 is registered Phase 3 with an ACTUAL enrolment of 2 (the book's trials table), which says the funnel is as thin as the pool above implies
